items.followUp: State two physical properties of metals.

rubric.why: A common physical property of non-metals is that they conduct heat or electricity poorly.
rubric.description: Identifies poor conductivity.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that non-metals are poor conductors of heat or electricity.

rubric.why: Non-metals have several other characteristic physical properties.
rubric.description: Gives another valid physical property.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for any one further correct property.

modelAnswer: Non-metals are generally poor conductors of heat and electricity.
Solid non-metals are brittle and are neither malleable nor ductile.
They are usually dull and non-sonorous.
(Any two properties.)

items.followUp: Name any two highly reactive metals.

rubric.why: These are among the least reactive metals commonly given in school chemistry.
rubric.description: Names one least reactive metal.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for one correct example.

rubric.why: A second valid example completes the response.
rubric.description: Names a second, different least reactive metal.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for a different correct example.

modelAnswer: Gold and platinum are two of the least reactive metals.

items.followUp: Describe one application each of Biochemistry and Industrial Chemistry.

rubric.why: This states what Biochemistry studies.
rubric.description: Defines Biochemistry.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for explaining that it studies chemical substances or processes in living organisms.

rubric.why: Biochemistry has practical applications in several fields.
rubric.description: Gives an application of Biochemistry.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for one relevant application.

accept: manufacture of chemicals on a commercial scale
chemical manufacture on a large scale
rubric.why: Industrial Chemistry concerns the commercial-scale production of chemicals and products.
rubric.description: Defines Industrial Chemistry.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for describing the manufacture of chemicals or products on a commercial or large scale.

rubric.why: These are examples of industries that use Industrial Chemistry.
rubric.description: Gives one industrial application or product.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for one valid industry or product.

rubric.why: A further example shows another field where Industrial Chemistry is used.
rubric.description: Gives a second industrial application or product.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for a different valid industry or product.

modelAnswer: Biochemistry is the study of chemical substances and processes in living organisms.
It is used in fields such as medicine, agriculture and food science.
For example, biochemical knowledge helps in understanding diseases and developing medicines.
Industrial Chemistry deals with the manufacture of chemicals and useful products on a commercial scale.
It is used in industries that produce fertilizers, cement, glass, soaps, paper and textiles.

items.followUp: Explain coordinate covalent bond formation in the ammonium ion and give one other example.

rubric.why: A coordinate covalent bond is a shared electron pair supplied by one atom.
rubric.description: States that the bond contains a shared pair of electrons.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for identifying the shared electron pair.

rubric.why: The defining feature is that one atom supplies both bonding electrons to an electron-deficient acceptor.
rubric.description: Explains donor-to-acceptor formation.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that one atom donates its lone pair to an atom or ion with a vacant orbital.

rubric.why: Ammonium ion formation is a standard example of coordinate bonding.
rubric.description: Gives the ammonium-ion example.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the formation of NH4+ from NH3 and H+.

rubric.why: Hydronium ion formation is another standard example.
rubric.description: Gives a second example.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the formation of H3O+ from H2O and H+.

modelAnswer: A coordinate covalent bond forms when one atom donates both electrons of a shared pair to another atom or ion.
The donating atom has a lone pair, and the acceptor has a vacant orbital.
For example, NH3 donates a lone pair to H+ to form NH4+: NH3 + H+ → NH4+.
Similarly, H2O donates a lone pair to H+ to form H3O+: H2O + H+ → H3O+.

items.followUp: Compare Rutherford’s nuclear model with Bohr’s atomic model.

accept: most of atom is empty space
rubric.why: These are central features of Rutherford’s nuclear model.
rubric.description: States a feature of Rutherford’s model.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the small positive nucleus or the mostly empty space in the atom.

rubric.why: Rutherford proposed that electrons move around the central nucleus.
rubric.description: Describes electron motion in Rutherford’s model.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that electrons revolve around the nucleus.

rubric.why: Bohr added that electrons occupy specific, stable orbits with definite energies.
rubric.description: States Bohr’s fixed-orbit concept.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for identifying definite orbits or energy levels.

accept: no energy radiated in stationary orbit
do not lose energy in fixed orbits
energy emitted or absorbed during transition
rubric.why: Bohr’s model explains atomic stability and energy changes through electron transitions.
rubric.description: Explains Bohr’s account of energy and stability.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that electrons do not radiate energy in stationary orbits and/or that energy changes occur during transitions.

rubric.why: Rutherford’s model could not account for atomic stability or line spectra, while Bohr’s model explained the hydrogen spectrum.
rubric.description: Compares the explanatory limits or success of the models.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for identifying a limitation of Rutherford’s model or a relevant success of Bohr’s model.

modelAnswer: Rutherford proposed that an atom has a small, positively charged nucleus and that most of the atom is empty space.
Electrons revolve around the nucleus.
Rutherford’s model could not explain why revolving electrons do not lose energy and fall into the nucleus, or explain line spectra.
Bohr proposed that electrons move in fixed orbits, each with a definite energy.
Electrons do not radiate energy in these stationary orbits; they absorb or emit energy when they move between orbits, explaining the hydrogen spectrum.

items.followUp: Explain how temperature, concentration and particle size affect the rate of diffusion in liquids.

rubric.why: Heating increases particle motion and speeds up diffusion.
rubric.description: Explains the effect of temperature.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that higher temperature makes diffusion faster.

rubric.why: A greater concentration difference drives faster net diffusion.
rubric.description: Explains the effect of concentration difference.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that a greater concentration gradient increases the rate.

rubric.why: Smaller or lighter particles generally diffuse more rapidly through a liquid.
rubric.description: Explains the effect of particle size or mass.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that smaller or lighter particles diffuse faster.

rubric.why: Diffusion is faster when particles move through a less resistant medium.
rubric.description: Explains the effect of liquid resistance or density.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for a correct explanation involving lower viscosity or lower density.

modelAnswer: Increasing the temperature increases the kinetic energy of liquid particles, so diffusion becomes faster.
A greater concentration difference between two regions increases the rate of diffusion.
Smaller or lighter particles diffuse faster than larger or heavier particles.
Diffusion is faster in a less viscous liquid because the particles can move through it more easily.

items.followUp: State four characteristics of a true solution.

rubric.why: A solution has uniform composition throughout.
rubric.description: Identifies the homogeneous nature of a solution.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that a solution is homogeneous or uniform throughout.

rubric.why: Solution particles are extremely small and cannot be seen with the naked eye.
rubric.description: Describes the small size of solution particles.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that the particles are very small or not visible.

rubric.why: Solution particles remain dispersed and do not settle on standing.
rubric.description: States that a solution is stable.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that particles do not settle on standing.

rubric.why: Dissolved particles pass through ordinary filter paper.
rubric.description: States the filtration property.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that a solution cannot be separated by ordinary filtration.

modelAnswer: A solution is a homogeneous mixture with uniform composition throughout.
Its solute particles are very small and cannot be seen with the naked eye.
The particles do not settle on standing, so the solution is stable.
The solute cannot be separated from the solution by ordinary filtration.

items.followUp: Differentiate between molecular mass and gram molecular mass.

rubric.why: Molecular mass is the sum of the atomic masses in one molecule and is expressed in atomic mass units.
rubric.description: Defines molecular mass and its unit.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that molecular mass is the sum of atomic masses expressed in u or amu.

rubric.why: Gram molecular mass is the molecular mass expressed in grams and represents the mass of one mole of molecules.
rubric.description: Defines gram molecular mass and distinguishes its unit or amount.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that it is the molecular mass in grams or the mass of one mole of molecules.

modelAnswer: Molecular mass is the sum of the atomic masses of the atoms in a molecule, expressed in atomic mass units (u).
Gram molecular mass is the molecular mass expressed in grams; it is the mass of one mole of molecules.
Their numerical values are equal, but their units differ.
